podcast.title: Founding Member of The Ramones
podcast.body: In 1973, after visiting Manie's Music with John Cummings to buy instruments, Douglas Colvin (who later became D.D. Ramone) formed The Ramones a year later with John (Johnny Ramone), Joey, and Tommy. The purchase of a guitar, a bass, and a small amp from the store was a direct precursor to the band's formation. "A year later, Douglas was calling himself D.D. and Johnny was Johnny. And together with Joey and Tommy, they formed the Ramones."

xref.title: Dee Dee King Rap Career (1987) – Hip-Hop Single "Funky Man" as Career Nadir
xref.body: In 1987, founding Ramones bassist Dee Dee Ramone abruptly left the band to pursue a solo hip-hop career under the name Dee Dee King, recording a track called "Funky Man." The attempt was widely considered disastrous. He tried to re-enter punk rock but never achieved significant success in any subsequent project. He died of a heroin overdose on June 5, 2002. "Dee Dee Ramon, the guy who played bass in all those legendary early Ramones songs, trying to be a rapper. Terrible career move, dude."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Deaths of Original Members (2001-2014)
xref.body: The original lineup of the Ramones tragically passed away over a 13-year period: Joey Ramone in 2001, Dee Dee Ramone in 2002, Johnny Ramone in 2004, and Tommy Ramone in 2014, marking the end of an era for the seminal punk band. "He was the first of the original Ramones to die. Base player DD Ramon died of a heroin overdose the following summer. Whereas Johnny Ramon lost his fight with prostate cancer in September 2004, and drummer Tommy Ramon was taken by Bile Duck Cancer in the summer of 2014."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Dee Dee Ramone – Self-Taught "Primitive" Bassist and Primary Lyricist
xref.body: Dee Dee Ramone came to the bass without prior knowledge of how to play it, embodying the punk ethos of "anyone can do it." Despite his basic technique, he became the Ramones' primary lyricist and a massive influence on a generation of musicians. His primitive approach was not a limitation but a defining feature. "A 'primitive' bassist who, without initially knowing how to play, embodied the punk spirit of 'anyone can do it' and was the band's main lyricist."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Dee Dee Ramone's Death and Memorial
xref.body: Dee Dee Ramone, who left the band in 1989 to pursue a solo career, play with other bands, and write a book, was found dead of a heroin overdose by his wife at his Hollywood apartment on June 5, 2002. He was 50 years old and is buried in the Hollywood Forever Cemetery. "On June 5, 2002, he was found dead of a heroin overdose by his wife at his department in Hollywood."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Dee Dee Ramone's Difficult Background
xref.body: Douglas Colvin (Dee Dee Ramone) grew up as an "army brat" in a profoundly unhappy military family, where domestic violence was common. After living on various American military bases in Germany, he moved to New York, where he descended into drug use and resorted to prostitution to fund his addiction. "Douglas was an army brat from a very unhappy military family where domestic violence was the order of the day."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Dee Dee Ramone's Mental Health and Mood Swings
xref.body: Dee Dee Ramone was reportedly diagnosed as bipolar but chose not to seek treatment. He was known as a "very scary dude prone to huge mood swings." "There's one story that he was diagnosed as being bipolar, but he didn't seek any treatment for it."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Financial Struggles
xref.body: The band struggled financially despite constant touring and merchandise sales, earning only $750 to $1,000 per show. Each member was living on a mere $125 per week, with Dee Dee Ramone famously spending $100 of that on heroin. "Each member of the band was living on a hundred and twenty five dollars a week."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Name Origin (Paul McCartney Connection)
xref.body: The band's chosen surname, "Ramone," was inspired by Dee Dee Ramone's admiration for Paul McCartney. During his time with The Silver Beatles, McCartney would use the alias "Paul Ramone" to check into hotel rooms. Dee Dee, already calling himself Dee Dee Ramone, suggested "The Ramones" for the band to signify unity and family. "DD was a big fan of Paul McCartney and the Beatles, and the days of the Silver Beatles, Paul McCartney used to check on two hotel rooms using the alias Paul Ramone."

xref.title: Stage Names and Image
xref.body: To symbolize their unity and brotherhood, all band members adopted the surname "Ramone." Jeff Hyman became Joey Ramone, Douglas Colvin became Dee Dee Ramone, John Cummings became Johnny Ramone, and Tommy kept his first name. They also adopted a uniform "tough leather jacket and jeans look." "Everybody adopted a tough leather jacket and jeans look, and everybody had a stage name. Jeff became Joey. Douglas was DD, John was Johnny, and Tommy stayed Tommy. And as a symbol of their brotherhood, they all adopted the same last name, Ramone."
